--- title: "Demographics" --- Population, age, race and ethnicity, household composition, and income for the Richmond region, from the ACS 5-year estimates. Every trend compares three non-overlapping five-year windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. ## Growth was strongest in Chesterfield and the expansion ring ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-pop-growth-1.png){#fig-pop-growth fig-align='left' fig-alt='Horizontal bar chart of population growth between the 2014 and 2024 ACS windows for the 17 Richmond-region localities, Ashland town, and the pooled core, expansion ring, and region. Chesterfield and the expansion ring grow around 16 percent, Richmond city about 9 percent, and Henrico about 7 percent; the region as a whole grows about 11 percent.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The region added 129,174 people between the 2014 and 2024 windows, growing 10.7% to 1,341,248. - Chesterfield grew 16.5% and the four-locality expansion ring 15.5%, against 8.7% in Richmond city and 6.6% in Henrico. - New Kent was the fastest-growing of the 17 localities (30.8%); Sussex was the slowest (-9.7%). ::: {#tbl-pop .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: - The three core localities hold 70.3% of the region's population, and Chesterfield alone is larger than either Henrico or Richmond city. - The expansion ring's 195,949 residents are about one-fifth of the core's, so its fast percentage growth is a smaller absolute gain than Chesterfield's. ## The region has outgrown Virginia in nearly every year since 2011 ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-pep-growth-1.png){#fig-pep-growth fig-align='left' fig-alt='Line chart of annual population growth rates, as a percent of the prior year\'s population, for the 17-locality Richmond region and for Virginia from 2011 to 2025, with a break at 2020 where the Census Bureau\'s estimates change vintage. The region grows between about 0.8 and 1.5 percent a year, peaking in 2024, and sits above the state line in every year but 2011; Virginia falls from about 1 percent to about 0.2 percent in 2022 before recovering.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Between 2011 and 2025 the 17-locality region grew faster than Virginia in 13 of 14 years. - The region's fastest year was 2024, when it grew 1.47% (19,910 people). - Virginia's growth slowed to 0.24% at its low point; the region never dropped below 0.74%. - Population Estimates Program figures and the ACS windows above measure different periods and use different methods, so their growth rates are not interchangeable. ## Migration, not births, now drives the region's growth ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-pep-components-1.png){#fig-pep-components fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked bar chart of annual components of population change for the Richmond region from 2011 to 2025, omitting 2020, with a diamond marking total population change each year. Natural change shrinks from about 4,000 to 5,000 a year in the early 2010s to under 2,000 a year after 2020, while international migration jumps to over 10,000 in 2024 and domestic migration holds at 6,000 to 7,500 a year.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Natural increase (births minus deaths) fell from 4,228 people a year in 2010-2019 to 1,451 a year in 2020-2025. - Net migration rose: 7,298 a year in 2010-2019 and 13,035 a year in 2020-2025, so it supplied 63% of growth in the first era and 90% in the second. - International migration peaked in 2024 at 10,787 people, well above any earlier year; domestic migration stayed between 6,069 and 7,543 a year after 2020. - In 10 of the 17 localities, deaths exceeded births over 2020-2025. ::: {#tbl-migration .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Population change and its components by era, July to July (2010-2019: nine years of components; 2020-2025: five). Migration share is net migration divided by population change; it can exceed 100% where natural change is negative. Source: Census Bureau Population Estimates Program, Vintages 2019 and 2025.
Geography Era Pop. change Natural change International Domestic Net migration Migration share
Richmond city 2010-2019 26,134 9,810 5,497 10,415 15,912 61%
Richmond city 2020-2025 10,330 3,658 7,887 -1,297 6,590 64%
Henrico 2010-2019 23,565 11,730 13,404 -1,375 12,029 51%
Henrico 2020-2025 7,846 1,338 11,714 -5,257 6,457 82%
Chesterfield 2010-2019 35,604 13,502 4,993 17,366 22,359 63%
Chesterfield 2020-2025 31,818 4,632 8,079 19,059 27,138 85%
Expansion ring 2010-2019 15,948 883 715 14,358 15,073 95%
Expansion ring 2020-2025 17,575 -1,058 881 17,708 18,589 106%
Richmond region 2010-2019 103,654 38,050 27,219 38,465 65,684 63%
Richmond region 2020-2025 72,655 7,254 30,105 35,071 65,176 90%
Virginia 2010-2019 511,820 332,270 255,828 -76,654 179,174 35%
Virginia 2020-2025 242,804 64,250 206,929 -29,143 177,786 73%
````` ::: ::: - The two eras are different lengths, so compare the per-year figures in the text rather than the era totals in the table. - The expansion ring is the clearest case: its natural change is negative in 2020-2025 (-1,058), so net migration (18,589) is more than all of its growth. ## Richmond city turned from domestic to international growth ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-mig-composition-1.png){#fig-mig-composition fig-align='left' fig-alt='Two-panel horizontal stacked bar chart of annual net migration per 1,000 residents, split into international and domestic migration, for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the expansion ring, the region, and Virginia, in 2010 to 2019 and 2020 to 2025. In Richmond city, domestic migration is positive in the first period and slightly negative in the second while international migration more than doubles. Henrico\'s domestic migration is negative in both periods. The expansion ring\'s net migration, almost entirely domestic, roughly doubles to about 19 per 1,000.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Richmond city's international migration rate rose from 2.8 to 6.8 per 1,000 residents a year, while its domestic rate swung from +5.3 to -1.1. - Henrico lost residents to domestic migration in both eras (-0.5 and -3.1) and grew on international migration (7.0 in 2020-2025). - Chesterfield's growth is mostly domestic movers: 10.0 domestic against 4.2 international per 1,000 in 2020-2025. - The expansion ring's net rate of 18.8 per 1,000 a year is almost entirely domestic (17.9). ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-mig-localities-1.png){#fig-mig-localities fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart of the annual net migration rate per 1,000 residents in 2010 to 2019 and 2020 to 2025 for the 17 Richmond-region localities, the region, and Virginia. Most localities\' rates rise in the second period; New Kent and Goochland are highest at above 30 per 1,000, while Petersburg is lowest, below zero.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Net migration rates rose in 14 of the 17 localities between 2010-2019 and 2020-2025; the highest in 2020-2025 were New Kent (36.6 per 1,000 a year) and Goochland (35.2). - The region's rate rose from 5.9 to 9.7 per 1,000, against 2.4 to 4.1 for Virginia. - The 3 localities whose rate was no higher in the 2020s than in the 2010s are Henrico, Prince George, and Richmond city. ::: callout-note ## How to read the migration estimates Population Estimates Program migration figures are **modeled from administrative records**, not counted, and are revised each vintage. Net migration is international plus domestic; domestic migration is the net balance of moves between this locality and the rest of the United States. The 2010-2019 and 2020-2025 series come from different vintages, the second built on the 2020 Census, so the page compares the eras instead of joining them. The 2010 and 2020 components cover only April to June and are omitted, and a small residual (not shown) accounts for the rest of each year's change. ::: ## The region is aging, and the expansion ring is aging fastest ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-age-1.png){#fig-age fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the share of population aged 65 and over in the three core Richmond localities, the pooled core, the pooled expansion ring, and the region across three ACS windows ending 2014, 2019, and 2024. The share rises in every geography; the expansion ring is highest, reaching 20 percent in 2024, and Richmond city is lowest at about 14 percent.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The region's 65-and-over share rose from 12.9% to 16.7%, while its under-18 share fell from 22.7% to 21.3%. - The expansion ring is the oldest geography: 20.0% are 65 or over, up +5.4 points since the 2014 window. - Richmond city is the youngest of the three core localities at 14.1% 65 and over, and has the smallest share of children of the three (17.5%). - Chesterfield has the largest share of children among the core three (23.7%), though that share also fell over the decade. ## Diversity grew across the region, but Richmond city moved the other way ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-race-1.png){#fig-race fig-align='left' fig-alt='Two-panel stacked horizontal bar chart of the share of population by race and ethnicity for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the pooled core, the pooled expansion ring, and the region, in the 2014 and 2024 ACS windows. White non-Hispanic share falls in the region, Henrico, Chesterfield, and the expansion ring, but edges up in Richmond city, where the Black share falls from about 49 to 41 percent. The Hispanic share rises in every geography.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The region's White non-Hispanic share fell from 58.7% to 54.7%; the Hispanic or Latino share rose from 5.5% to 8.4%. - Richmond city went the other direction: its White non-Hispanic share rose from 39.7% to 41.4%, and its Black share fell from 48.6% to 40.6%. - Chesterfield and Henrico diversified: their White non-Hispanic shares fell to 56.4% and 49.5%, and Henrico's Asian share reached 9.4%. - The expansion ring remains the least diverse geography, at 80.3% White non-Hispanic. ::: callout-note ## Read the multiracial change with care The "Multiracial" share roughly doubled in the region, but part of that is measurement, not demographic change. The Census Bureau revised how it codes and processes write-in race responses beginning with 2020 data, which raised the count of people classified as two or more races. The 2014 window predates that change and the 2024 window includes it, so treat the multiracial trend as partly methodological. ::: ::: {#tbl-race .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Share of population by race and ethnicity, 2024 ACS 5-year window, with the change since 2014 in percentage points in parentheses. Source: ACS Table B03002.
Race / ethnicity Richmond region Richmond core Richmond city Henrico Chesterfield Expansion ring

Hispanic or Latino 8.4% (+3.0) 9.8% (+3.4) 10.7% (+4.3) 6.9% (+1.7) 11.9% (+4.3) 3.8% (+1.5)
Asian 4.2% (+0.7) 5.3% (+0.8) 2.1% (-0.1) 9.4% (+2.4) 3.6% (+0.2) 1.7% (+0.6)
Multiracial 4.3% (+2.2) 4.4% (+2.1) 4.6% (+1.8) 4.4% (+2.1) 4.4% (+2.4) 4.1% (+2.4)
Another race 0.8% (+0.3) 0.8% (+0.3) 0.7% (+0.4) 0.7% (+0.3) 0.9% (+0.4) 0.7% (+0.2)
````` ::: ::: - Every geography's Hispanic or Latino share rose over the decade, from 2.3% to 3.8% in the expansion ring and from 7.6% to 11.9% in Chesterfield. - The Black share is the largest in Richmond city (40.6%) and smallest in the expansion ring (9.5%). ## Household makeup splits the same way: singles in the city, married couples in the ring ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-households-1.png){#fig-households fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked horizontal bar chart of households by type for Richmond city, Henrico, the pooled core, the region, Chesterfield, and the pooled expansion ring in 2024. People living alone are the largest group in Richmond city at 43 percent of households; married-couple families are the largest group in the expansion ring at 61 percent and in Chesterfield at 55 percent.' width=100%} ::: ::: - People living alone are 43.1% of Richmond city households, against 30.6% in Henrico, 22.9% in Chesterfield, and 21.1% in the expansion ring. - Married-couple families are 61.4% of expansion-ring households and 54.8% of Chesterfield's, but only 24.6% of Richmond city's. - Across the whole region, 29.6% of households are one person — a household type that often fits a smaller unit than the detached single-family homes that dominate the stock (see the Inventory page). ## After inflation, incomes rose in every geography, fastest in Richmond city among the core localities ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-income-real-1.png){#fig-income-real fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart of real median household income, in 2024 dollars, in the 2014 and 2024 ACS windows for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, four comparison metros, and Virginia. Income rises in every geography. Richmond city rises from about 55 thousand to about 65 thousand dollars, the Richmond metro from about 79 thousand to about 87 thousand, and the Washington metro stays highest at about 127 thousand.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The Richmond MSA's median household income rose 9.6% in real terms, from $79,075.41 to $86,679 in 2024 dollars (45.2% before adjusting for inflation). - Richmond city's real median income rose 17.9%, faster than Henrico (9.1%) and Chesterfield (6.1%), but at $64,587 it remains well below both. - The Richmond MSA ended the period close to Virginia's median ($86,679 against $93,170) and far below the Washington MSA ($126,684). ::: {#tbl-income .cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Median household income as published (each window's own dollars), with nominal and inflation-adjusted change, 2014 to 2024. Cells with a coefficient of variation above 30 are suppressed (—); * marks a medium-reliability estimate (CV 15-30). Source: ACS Table B19013.
Geography 2014 2024 Nominal change Real change
Washington MSA $91,756 $126,684 38.1% 4.2%
New Kent $73,030 $123,314 68.9% 27.4%
Goochland $82,460 $118,931 44.2% 8.8%
Hanover $77,550 $112,805 45.5% 9.8%
Powhatan $75,447 $110,537 46.5% 10.6%
Chesterfield $72,514 $101,931 40.6% 6.1%
Charlottesville MSA $59,189 $93,598 58.1% 19.3%
Virginia $64,792 $93,170 43.8% 8.5%
Henrico $61,438 $88,783 44.5% 9.1%
Richmond MSA $59,677 $86,679 45.2% 9.6%
Hampton Roads MSA $59,244 $82,330 39.0% 4.9%
Richmond city $41,331 $64,587 56.3% 17.9%
Ashland town $41,582 $61,164* 47.1% 11.0%
````` ::: ::: - Inflation consumed most of the nominal gain: the Richmond MSA's median rose 45.2% as published but only 9.6% after adjusting for prices. - Ashland's median ($61,164) is a small-town estimate with a wide margin of error; it carries a reliability marker in the table. ## Typical renters earn well under the typical household in every geography ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-income-renter-1.png){#fig-income-renter fig-align='left' fig-alt='Dumbbell chart of real median renter household income, in 2024 dollars, in the 2014 and 2024 ACS windows for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, four comparison metros, and Virginia. Renter income is well below the all-household figure everywhere. Richmond city rises from about 38 thousand to about 48 thousand dollars and the Richmond metro from about 48 thousand to about 55 thousand.' width=100%} ::: ::: - The Richmond MSA's median renter household income was $54,728 in 2024 dollars, 63.1% of the all-household median ($86,679). It rose 14.1% in real terms, against 9.6% for all households. - Among the core three, renter income is 74.6% of the all-household median in Richmond city, 67.1% in Henrico, and 61.1% in Chesterfield. Richmond city's real renter income rose 25.5%, Henrico's 10.7%, and Chesterfield's 5.5%. - This is the income the Market page and the summary set against home values and rents, because renters are the group that would be moving toward ownership. ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-income-bands-1.png){#fig-income-bands fig-align='left' fig-alt='Stacked horizontal bar chart of households by income band for Richmond city, Henrico, the pooled core, the region, Chesterfield, and the pooled expansion ring in 2024. About 20 percent of Richmond city households earn under 25 thousand dollars against about 8 percent in Chesterfield and the expansion ring, and about 34 percent of expansion-ring households earn 150 thousand or more against 18 percent in Richmond city.' width=100%} ::: ::: - 20.2% of Richmond city households earn under $25,000, against 8.4% in Chesterfield and 7.6% in the expansion ring. - At the top, 34.4% of expansion-ring households earn $150,000 or more, against 29.2% in Chesterfield and 18.1% in Richmond city. - Income bands are fixed nominal thresholds, so a rising share in the top band partly reflects inflation, not only real gains. ## Renter households skew far lower-income than owners ::: {.cell layout-align="left"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](demographics_files/figure-html/fig-tenure-income-1.png){#fig-tenure-income fig-align='left' fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of the share of households earning under 50 thousand dollars, by tenure, for Richmond city, Henrico, Chesterfield, the pooled core, the pooled expansion ring, and the region in 2024. Renter households are far more likely to earn under 50 thousand dollars than owners in every geography; in the region the shares are about 46 percent for renters and 19 percent for owners.' width=100%} ::: ::: - Across the region, 45.9% of renter households earn under $50,000, against 18.9% of owner households. - In Richmond city, 51.9% of renters and 24.0% of owners fall under that line. - Even in the expansion ring, where incomes are highest, 36.1% of renters earn under $50,000 — the rental market there serves a lower-income group than the ownership market does. ::: callout-warning ## Small-geography reliability Ashland and the four expansion-ring localities have much smaller samples than the core. 5 of the 30 race-and-ethnicity cells for those five geographies fall below the CV-30 reliability threshold in the 2024 window. Figures here use the pooled expansion-ring row, and tables suppress low-reliability cells (—) and mark medium-reliability ones (*). ::: ::: callout-tip ## What this page shows - **Growth:** the region grew 10.7%, led by Chesterfield and the expansion ring, and outgrew Virginia in 13 of 14 years. - **Migration:** net migration supplied 90% of regional growth in 2020-2025, as natural increase fell. - **Age:** the 65-and-over share rose in every geography, and the expansion ring is the oldest. - **Race and ethnicity:** the region diversified, but Richmond city's White share rose while its Black share fell. - **Households:** living alone dominates in Richmond city (43.1%); married couples dominate in the ring. - **Income:** real median income rose everywhere, and renters earn far less than owners (median renter income is 63.1% of the metro's all-household median) — the gap the market page turns into cost burden. :::
